knowledgeAnswers.rationale: Fourteen divided by 40 is 0.35, which is 35 per cent. Option 1 uses the raw count of repeat customers as if it were a percentage, and option 2 is the sample size.
Sampling variation means a different group of customers naturally gives a slightly different share, especially when the sample is small. Options 2 and 3 are not reasons a repeat share would move.

A 12-customer batch gives a rough estimate with a wide margin. The sensible response is to keep counting over longer windows. A fixed-fact reading overstates what 12 customers show, and discarding the result throws away information.

practicalCriteria: The learner writes a definition of repeat customer that a colleague could apply to the same records and get the same count.
Using at least 30 records, the learner calculates a repeat share and reports it with the window and the sample size.
The learner splits the sample into two batches, recalculates each share and explains the difference in their own words, including what it does and does not support.
passRule: 80% on knowledge checks; practical sign-off separate
evidenceRequired: Written definition with the date it was set
Worksheet showing the counts, window, share, sample size and two-batch comparison
Assessor observation of the learner explaining sampling variation
stopWorkCriteria: Stop and do not report a rate if the definition has changed partway through the window without a note explaining why.
Stop if the customer records cannot be shared or stored in line with privacy duties that have been checked.
